meaning: The high god of the Canaanite pantheon; the common Semitic word for "god" and a divine name

phonemes.desc: Glottal stop [ʔ] plus long [eː], marked by macron; the long vowel distinguishes the divine name from the common noun 'god' in some forms.
Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l]; the root ʾil- means 'god, divine power' throughout Semitic.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AYLE' — like 'ale' with a long vowel and a slight glottal catch at the beginning; the name is short and resonant.

kin.label: Ugaritic
kin.form: 𐎛𐎍 (ʾil), the high god; also 𐎛𐎍𐎁 (ʾil ʾib), 'god of the father' / divine ancestor

kin.label: Hebrew
kin.form: אֵל (ʾĒl), 'God' or the name El; preserved in Israel, Bethel, Gabriel, Michael

pronunciation.note: Ēl is both a proper name and the common Semitic word for 'god.' The macron marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֵל and Ugaritic spellings. As a Tier-1 name it preserves length (macron) — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: Father of Years, Bull of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Supreme God, Creator, and King of the Divine Assembly
domains.lead: Ēl is the ancient one at the center of the Canaanite pantheon. He is the father of gods and men, the Bull whose creative power generates the divine assembly, and the king whose distant authority nonetheless settles every dispute. Unlike Baꜥal, who acts, Ēl decrees. His throne is at the source of the rivers; his tent is where the gods come to receive judgment.

cards.name: Creator of Creatures
cards.desc: His epithet bny bnwt, 'Creator of Creatures,' marks him as the ultimate source of all life.

cards.name: Bull El
cards.desc: The bull is his animal: strength, fertility, and patriarchal authority concentrated in one image.

cards.name: King and Judge
cards.desc: The divine assembly gathers before him; kingship is conferred by his word, whether for Baꜥal or for Athtar.

cards.name: Father of Gods and Men
cards.desc: He is 'ab ʾilm, 'father of the gods,' and 'ab ʾadmi, 'father of man' — the origin of all genealogies.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: 'Bull El' — ṯr ʾil — the patriarch's strength and fertility concentrated in a single animal image

symbols.name: Grey beard
symbols.meaning: ʾab šnm, 'father of years' — the venerable wisdom that outlasts every storm god

symbols.name: Source of rivers
symbols.meaning: The ʾapq rḥm, the confluence of the cosmic freshwater springs beneath his tent

symbols.name: Winged sun or throne
symbols.meaning: The exalted kingship of the divine council over which he presides

mythology.lead: Ēl appears in almost every major Ugaritic myth, yet he rarely takes center stage. He is the one appealed to, the one who gives or withholds blessing, the one whose laughter signals cosmic assent. His mythology is the mythology of authority itself — distant, benevolent, sometimes foolish, always final.

myths.title: The Kingmaker of the Assembly
myths.text: Twice in the Baꜥal Cycle the fate of the cosmos turns on a decree from Ēl's tent. First, persuaded by an appeal from the Sea, he grants kingship to Yamm, whose messengers then march into the assembly demanding Baꜥal as a captive (KTU 1.2 i–iii). Baꜥal's partisans seethe, but nothing moves until the old god speaks again. Much later, cajoled by his consort Asherah, Ēl grants Baꜥal the palace and the throne (KTU 1.4 iv–v). Even the mighty storm god, it turns out, rules only by the father's permission. The cycle makes an austere point about authority: Ēl never fights, never journeys, rarely leaves the source of the rivers, yet every coronation in heaven requires his word. Warrior gods can win the world; only the father of years can make a victory legitimate.

myths.title: Father of Years at the Source of the Rivers
myths.text: The poets give Ēl epithets no younger god can claim: ʾab šnm, 'Father of Years,' and bny bnwt, 'Creator of Creatures.' His dwelling is a tent pitched where the cosmic rivers rise, the ʾapq rḥm — the confluence of the freshwater springs beneath the world. When divine messengers seek him, they find him gracious, convivial, generous with blessing — and slow. The high god can even afford comedy: in KTU 1.114 he presides over a banquet, drinks himself insensible on wine, and must be carried home through the fields, while Aštart and ꜥAnat stagger along beside him and the moon god taunts him. The scene is funny; the theology is not. Ēl's power does not depend on dignity, beauty, or vigilance. It rests on nothing but age and word — the authority of the one who was already old when the seasons began.

myths.title: The Dream of the Childless King
myths.text: At the low point of the Epic of Keret (KTU 1.14 i), the king weeps in his inner chamber: seven wives dead, his line broken, his house failing. Then Ēl comes to him in a dream and asks, 'Who is Keret, that he should weep...? Shall his harem die, his legitimate wives perish?' He instructs the king to march on the wealthy city of Udum and claim its princess, promising a house that will number seventy sons. Through three tablets the epic tests that promise — war, pestilence, a son's terrible curse — but its theology is set in the first scene: blessing, not battle magic, is Ēl's instrument, and it arrives uninvited to a weeping king. The poem is a window on Canaanite royal ideology. The legitimacy of a dynasty rested on the dream-voice of the father of gods, the only authority that could promise a king descendants 'like the stars of El.'

myths.title: The Shameless Procreator
myths.text: KTU 1.23 is among the strangest tablets from Ras Shamra: fragmentary, partly obscene, and tied to a rite of first fruits. In its mythic frame, Ēl, creator of creatures, sees two women bathing by the sea and seduces them 'in the best way and the worst way' — Wyatt's celebrated rendering of a phrase translators have wrestled with for a century. Later scenes show him in his palace, entangled with his wives, while the newborn Gracious Gods — Shahar and Shalim, Dawn and Dusk — demand meat and drink with an appetite compared to Death itself. Because the tablet is broken, scholars still dispute how the scenes connect. What is clear is the theology of fertility: the high god's sexuality is no scandal but the engine of the agricultural year, and even the hungriest newborn gods must finally be fed into goodness.

lore.syncretism: Ēl is the common Semitic god par excellence. His name underlies Hebrew ʾĒl and its compounds (Israel, Gabriel, Michael), and it survives in Arabic Allāh (< al-ʾilāh, 'the God'). In the Greek world, the Phoenician high god was identified with Kronos, the aged father of Zeus, while Baꜥal was compared to Zeus himself. In Hurrian and Hittite treaties, Ēl appears as Elkunirša, paired with Asherah/Ašertu. The biblical tradition eventually absorbed Ēl into Yahweh: many of Israel's oldest poems use ʾĒl as a name or title for their own god, and the epithet ʾĒl Shaddai may preserve a Canaanite title of the high god.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ēl did not disappear; he was subsumed. His name lives in the word 'God' itself across the Semitic languages, in countless theophoric personal names, and in the biblical title El Shaddai. The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is partly shaped by the old Canaanite high god: distant, paternal, creator, judge. In modern religious studies, Ēl has become a test case for how monotheism emerged not by inventing a new deity but by elevating and narrowing an old one. To name Ēl is therefore to name an ancestor shared by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — and by the Canaanite religion they eventually superseded.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ēl is the god of 'and then what?' He does not rush into battle; he sits at the source of the rivers and lets the younger gods come to him. His authority is so settled that he can afford to be slow, even tipsy, even outmaneuvered by his own wife and children. Yet when he speaks, the cosmos arranges itself around his word.

There is a kind of spiritual maturity in Ēl that the modern world often undervalues. He represents the authority that does not need to prove itself, the father who does not compete with his children, the creator who can delegate the storm to Baꜥal without jealousy. To meditate on Ēl is to ask whether our own craving for action, novelty, and recognition allows room for the older, slower power that holds everything together.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎛𐎍 (ʾ-i-l), the common word for 'god' as well as the proper name of the high god. Phoenician writes 𐤀𐤋 (ʾ-l). The macron over ē in Ēl marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֵל and from comparative Semitic evidence. The name is both appellative and proper name, a fact that makes Ēl uniquely elusive and foundational.

lore.archaeology: At Ugarit the Baʿal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6) and the Epic of Keret (KTU 1.14–1.16) name ʾil as supreme judge and royal patron. The Karatepe bilingual invokes El as creator of the earth. Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions preserve El names in an Israelite religious context, while Tel Arad ostraca, Shechem, and Jerusalem temple texts show his continued prestige. His name underlies Biblical ʾĒl, ʾĒl ʿElyôn, and theophoric names such as Israel and Gabriel.
